vignette: A 22-year-old motorcyclist suffers a traction injury to his shoulder. On examination, the right upper extremity hangs limply at his side in adduction, internal rotation, and forearm pronation (the 'waiter's tip' position). There is profound weakness of shoulder abduction, external rotation, and elbow flexion. The biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are absent. Sensation is impaired over the lateral shoulder, lateral arm, and radial forearm.
question: Which portion of the brachial plexus is injured in Erb-Duchenne palsy?
options: Lower trunk (C8-T1 roots/trunk)
Posterior cord
Medial cord
Upper trunk (C5-C6 roots/trunk)
Lateral cord

explanation.why_correct: Erb-Duchenne palsy involves the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5-C6 ventral rami). Paralysis affects the deltoid and supraspinatus (loss of abduction), infraspinatus and teres minor (loss of external rotation), biceps and brachialis (loss of elbow flexion), and supinator (forearm pronation). Unopposed adductors, internal rotators, and pronators create the classic 'waiter's tip' posture, with sensory loss in C5-C6 dermatomes and lost biceps/brachioradialis reflexes.
distractors: Lower trunk plexopathy (Klumpke palsy, C8-T1) affects intrinsic hand muscles causing a claw hand, frequently with an associated Horner syndrome.
Posterior cord lesions cause weakness of shoulder abduction (axillary) and elbow/wrist extension (radial), but spare the musculocutaneous-innervated biceps.
Medial cord lesions impair ulnar and medial-median innervated muscles without affecting shoulder abduction or biceps flexion.
Lateral cord lesions impair the musculocutaneous nerve, but spare axillary (deltoid) and suprascapular (supraspinatus/infraspinatus) muscles, which arise directly from the trunk/posterior elements.
explanation.key_point: Upper trunk (Erb-Duchenne, C5-C6) plexopathy produces the 'waiter's tip' limb posture with lost shoulder abduction, external rotation, and elbow flexion.

section: Lower Trunk Brachial Plexopathy vs TOS
vignette: A 54-year-old woman with a history of apical lung carcinoma presents with progressive weakness and wasting of all intrinsic muscles of the right hand. Neurologic examination shows a claw hand deformity, marked atrophy of both thenar and hypothenar muscles, and sensory loss along the medial hand, medial forearm, and distal medial arm. In addition, there is mild ptosis and pupillary miosis of the right eye with preserved sweating on the face.
question: Why does a lower trunk brachial plexopathy frequently produce an associated Horner syndrome?
options: The sympathetic trunk runs directly inside the axillary sheath with the posterior cord
The lesion compresses the brainstem hypothalamospinal sympathetic tract
The stellate ganglion is directly innervated by the radial nerve
Preganglionic sympathetic T1 fibers join the lower trunk as they exit the spinal cord through the T1 ventral ramus
Microvascular ischemia to the carotid bifurcation sympathetics

explanation.why_correct: The lower trunk of the brachial plexus is formed by the union of the C8 and T1 ventral rami. Sympathetic preganglionic fibers destined for the head and eye exit the spinal cord in the T1 ventral ramus before ascending to the superior cervical ganglion. Apical thoracic tumors (Pancoast tumor) compressing the lower trunk invariably disrupt these T1 sympathetic fibers, producing an ipsilateral Horner syndrome alongside C8-T1 intrinsic hand wasting.
distractors: The sympathetic chain lies paravertebrally over the rib necks and apical pleura, not within the distal axillary sheath.
Brainstem hypothalamospinal tract lesions produce Horner syndrome with crossed body analgesia or other central brainstem signs, not isolated hand wasting.
The radial nerve is derived from C5-T1 posterior cord and has no connection with the stellate sympathetic ganglion.
Carotid bifurcation lesions produce third-order postganglionic Horner syndrome, which spares facial sweating but does not cause plexus hand wasting.
explanation.key_point: Lower trunk brachial plexopathy (C8-T1) commonly causes an ipsilateral Horner syndrome because preganglionic sympathetic axons travel in the T1 ventral ramus.

vignette: A 38-year-old previously healthy man develops excruciating, deep, boring pain in his right shoulder that wakes him from sleep and persists for 5 days. As the pain subsides, he notices that his right scapula protrudes backwards when pushing against a wall. Examination reveals medial winging of the right scapula and profound weakness of the serratus anterior muscle. Sensation is minimally decreased over the lateral shoulder, and the rest of the arm is intact.
question: What is the diagnosis and anatomical structure predominantly involved?
options: C5 cervical radiculopathy due to acute disk herniation
Suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch
Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome) with long thoracic nerve involvement
Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) injury from lymph node biopsy
Thoracic outlet syndrome

explanation.why_correct: Neuralgic amyotrophy (brachial amyotrophy / Parsonage-Turner syndrome) is an acute idiopathic/immune-mediated inflammatory plexopathy characterized by sudden severe unrelenting shoulder/arm pain lasting days to weeks, followed rapidly by patchy weakness and denervation atrophy as pain abates. The long thoracic nerve (supplying the serratus anterior, causing medial scapular winging) is the most commonly affected isolated nerve, followed by the anterior interosseous and suprascapular nerves.
distractors: C5 radiculopathy causes prominent deltoid and biceps weakness with diminished biceps reflex, not isolated medial scapular winging.
Suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch causes isolated infraspinatus weakness (external rotation deficit) without scapular winging.
Spinal accessory nerve injury paralyses the trapezius, producing lateral (not medial) scapular winging with downward and outward displacement.
Thoracic outlet syndrome causes chronic progressive thenar wasting and ulnar sensory complaints, not acute nocturnal severe shoulder pain.
explanation.key_point: Parsonage-Turner syndrome presents with acute severe shoulder pain followed by patchy motor weakness, most frequently targeting the long thoracic nerve (medial scapular winging).

source_quote: results from damage to the fifth and sixth cervical roots or the upper trunk of the brachial plexus
vignette: A neonate born via complicated breech delivery with shoulder dystocia presents with a right arm adducted at the shoulder, internally rotated, elbow extended, and forearm pronated ('waiter's tip' posture). The Moro and biceps reflexes are absent on that side.
question: Which roots and trunk of the brachial plexus are injured?
options: C8 and T1 roots (Lower trunk of brachial plexus — Klumpke palsy)
C5 and C6 roots (Upper trunk of brachial plexus — Erb-Duchenne palsy)
Middle trunk (C7 root) causing isolated triceps and extensor paralysis
Posterior cord injury affecting radial and axillary nerves

explanation.why_correct: Traction on the neck during delivery ruptures or stretches the upper trunk (C5–C6), paralyzing the deltoid, supraspinatus/infraspinatus, biceps, and brachioradialis, yielding the classic 'waiter's tip' posture.
distractors: Lower trunk (C8–T1) Klumpke palsy involves intrinsic hand muscles with a claw hand and often an ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
Middle trunk (C7) lesions selectively impair triceps and forearm extensors without the classic Erb posture.
Posterior cord lesions cause axillary (deltoid) and radial weakness but spare biceps and supraspinatus.
explanation.key_point: Erb-Duchenne palsy involves C5–C6 (upper trunk), producing the 'waiter's tip' deformity with adducted, internally rotated shoulder and extended, pronated elbow.

source_quote: the lower brachial plexus is initially affected, resulting in pain in the ulnar side of the hand, forearm, and arm
vignette: A 56-year-old woman with a history of apical lung carcinoma presents with progressive left hand weakness, severe pain along the medial forearm, and clawing of the fingers. Examination reveals partial ptosis and miosis of the left eye with anhidrosis of the left face.
question: Which plexus structure is compromised to explain both the claw hand and Horner syndrome?
options: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) in contact with the cervical sympathetic chain (Pancoast tumor)
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5–C6) compressing the suprascapular nerve
Lateral cord of the brachial plexus anterior to the axillary artery
Posterior cord of the brachial plexus within the axilla

explanation.why_correct: Pancoast tumors invade the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) and the adjacent stellate ganglion, producing total intrinsic hand weakness (claw hand) and an ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
distractors: Upper trunk lesions spare intrinsic hand muscles and do not cause Horner syndrome.
The lateral cord gives rise to the musculocutaneous and lateral median roots and does not cause a claw hand or Horner syndrome.
Posterior cord lesions involve radial, axillary, and thoracodorsal nerves, leaving autonomic sympathetic fibers unaffected.
explanation.key_point: Lower trunk brachial plexopathy combined with Horner syndrome is pathognomonic of an apical superior sulcus (Pancoast) lesion.

source_quote: weakness of thigh flexion (iliopsoas), leg extension (quadriceps), thigh eversion (sartorius), and thigh adduction (adductor muscles)
vignette: A 62-year-old diabetic man develops sudden excruciating deep aching pain in his right anterior thigh, followed days later by marked weakness in hip flexion (iliopsoas 2/5), knee extension (quadriceps 2/5), and hip adduction (adductor longus 2/5). His patellar reflex is absent.
question: Why does weakness of the hip adductors confirm a lumbar plexopathy rather than an isolated femoral neuropathy?
options: Adductor longus is innervated by the superior gluteal nerve arising from the sacral plexus
Adductor longus is innervated by the obturator nerve (L2–L4), which originates from the lumbar plexus alongside the femoral nerve
Femoral nerve directly innervates all medial thigh adductors in the femoral triangle
Adductors are supplied exclusively by the sciatic nerve trunk

explanation.why_correct: The obturator nerve (L2–L4) innervates the adductor group. Because the femoral nerve does not innervate the adductors, weakness of both quadriceps (femoral) and adductors (obturator) proves a proximal lumbar plexus lesion.
distractors: The superior gluteal nerve innervates gluteus medius and minimus (hip abductors), not the adductor longus.
The femoral nerve innervates the quadriceps, sartorius, and pectineus, not the main adductor mass.
The sciatic nerve innervates the hamstrings and muscles below the knee.
explanation.key_point: Weakness of hip adductors (obturator nerve) combined with quadriceps weakness (femoral nerve) definitively localizes the lesion to the lumbar plexus.

source_quote: The pain is followed within several hours to days by paresis of the shoulder and, predominantly, proximal arm musculature.
vignette: A 35-year-old marathon runner experiences acute, severe, relentless burning pain in the right shoulder and periscapular region. Two weeks later, as the pain subsides, he develops marked scapular winging and profound weakness in shoulder abduction.
question: What is the diagnosis?
options: C5 cervical disc herniation with acute motor radiculopathy
Rotator cuff tear with secondary subacromial bursitis
Parsonage-Turner syndrome (acute idiopathic brachial plexopathy / neuralgic amyotrophy)
Thoracic outlet syndrome with subclavius entrapment

explanation.why_correct: Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy) is characterized by acute severe unilateral shoulder pain lasting days to weeks, rapidly followed by patchy multifocal muscle weakness and amyotrophy (often involving long thoracic or suprascapular nerves).
distractors: C5 radiculopathy causes pain radiating along the lateral arm, not severe periscapular burning followed by patchy serratus/deltoid paralysis.
Rotator cuff tears cause mechanical pain with movement, not severe unprovoked neuropathic pain followed by scapular winging.
Thoracic outlet syndrome causes chronic aching and numbness along the ulnar border of the forearm and hand (C8-T1).
explanation.key_point: Severe unprovoked shoulder pain that resolves only to give way to severe patchy weakness and wasting is the classic biphasic signature of Parsonage-Turner syndrome.

vignette: Following a carotid endarterectomy, a 68-year-old man notes numbness over his angle of the jaw and earlobe. Neurological exam reveals preserved facial nerve motor function, but sensory loss over the skin of the parotid region, mastoid process, and lower pinna.
question: Which branch of the cervical plexus was traumatized?
options: Transverse cervical nerve (C2–C3)
Lesser occipital nerve (C2)
Great auricular nerve (C2–C3)
Supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4)

explanation.why_correct: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) curves around the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle to supply sensation to the lower earlobe, angle of the mandible, and parotid area; it is vulnerable during carotid surgery.
distractors: The transverse cervical nerve innervates the anterior triangle of the neck.
The lesser occipital nerve supplies the scalp behind and superior to the ear.
The supraclavicular nerves supply the skin over the clavicle and upper chest down to the second rib.
explanation.key_point: Sensory loss over the angle of the jaw and lower pinna following carotid surgery reflects injury to the great auricular nerve (cervical plexus C2–C3).

source_quote: Paralysis of this nerve results in loss of diaphragmatic movement on the affected side. When unilateral, this paralysis results in little disability at rest
vignette: A 61-year-old man develops exertional dyspnea after open-heart surgery, but he is comfortable at rest. Fluoroscopy shows that the right hemidiaphragm fails to descend during inspiration and is drawn upward. There is no weakness of the arms or neck.
question: Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5)
Long thoracic nerve (C5-C7)
Spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI)
Dorsal scapular nerve (C4-C5)
Ansa cervicalis (C1-C3)

explanation.why_correct: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) innervates the diaphragm. Unilateral paralysis causes little disability at rest but exertional dyspnea, and the affected hemidiaphragm fails to descend with inspiration and may be drawn upward. Open-heart surgery is a recognized cause of phrenic injury.
distractors: The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior, so its lesion produces scapular winging, not diaphragmatic paralysis.
The spinal accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, not the diaphragm.
The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the levator scapulae and rhomboids.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid muscles, not the diaphragm.
explanation.key_point: Unilateral phrenic palsy: little disability at rest, exertional dyspnea, and a hemidiaphragm that fails to descend or moves paradoxically upward.

source_quote: The seventh cervical fibers to the radial nerve are primarily involved, and therefore, the extensors of the forearm, hand, and fingers are paretic
vignette: A 33-year-old man has weakness of elbow extension and of wrist and finger extension after a fall. Elbow flexion and shoulder abduction are normal. The triceps reflex is depressed, and sensation is patchily reduced over the extensor forearm and the radial side of the back of the hand.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
Middle trunk of the brachial plexus
Lower trunk of the brachial plexus
Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
Posterior cord of the brachial plexus

explanation.why_correct: The middle trunk carries C7 fibers destined mainly for the radial nerve, so the extensors of the forearm, hand and fingers are paretic and the triceps reflex is depressed. Elbow flexion is spared because brachioradialis and brachialis are supplied mainly by C5-C6.
distractors: An upper trunk lesion (C5-C6) weakens deltoid, biceps, brachioradialis and brachialis and depresses the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes; shoulder abduction and elbow flexion are normal here.
A lower trunk lesion (C8-T1) weakens wrist and finger flexors and intrinsic hand muscles, with medial sensory loss.
A lateral cord lesion affects musculocutaneous and lateral median-innervated muscles (elbow flexion, pronation, wrist flexion), not the extensors.
A posterior cord lesion would also involve the axillary, subscapular and thoracodorsal nerves, so shoulder abduction would be weak.
explanation.key_point: A middle trunk (C7) lesion paralyzes the radial-innervated extensors and triceps reflex while sparing elbow flexion.

source_quote: paresis of all muscles innervated by the median nerve except the intrinsic hand muscles
vignette: A 40-year-old woman has weakness of elbow flexion, forearm pronation and radial wrist flexion after shoulder surgery. The biceps reflex is absent, and there is sensory loss over the lateral forearm. The intrinsic hand muscles, triceps and deltoid are strong.
question: Which part of the brachial plexus is injured?
options: Medial cord
Posterior cord
Upper trunk
Lateral cord
Lower trunk

explanation.why_correct: The lateral cord gives the musculocutaneous nerve (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis; lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) and the lateral head of the median nerve, so all median-innervated muscles except the intrinsic hand muscles are weak. The biceps reflex is depressed or absent.
distractors: A medial cord lesion affects ulnar-innervated and median-innervated intrinsic hand muscles, which are spared here.
A posterior cord lesion affects the subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves (deltoid, triceps, wrist and finger extensors), which are normal here.
An upper trunk lesion would also weaken the deltoid and spinati and spare the median-innervated forearm pronators and wrist flexors.
A lower trunk lesion (C8-T1) weakens finger flexors and intrinsic hand muscles, which are spared here.
explanation.key_point: Lateral cord lesions weaken musculocutaneous and lateral-head median muscles (everything median except the intrinsic hand muscles) and depress the biceps reflex.

source_quote: Lesions of the posterior cord result in disability in the fields of distribution of the subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary, and radial nerves.
vignette: A 29-year-old man has weakness of shoulder abduction and external rotation, and of elbow, wrist and finger extension, after an axillary injury. Elbow flexion by the biceps is preserved. The triceps reflex is absent, with sensory loss over the lateral arm and the back of the hand.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus
Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
Medial cord of the brachial plexus
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
Middle trunk of the brachial plexus

explanation.why_correct: The posterior cord gives the subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves. Axillary involvement weakens the deltoid and teres minor with lateral arm sensory loss; radial involvement weakens elbow, wrist and finger extension and abolishes the triceps reflex.
distractors: A lateral cord lesion weakens the biceps and median-innervated forearm muscles, which are spared here.
A medial cord lesion affects ulnar and medial-head median intrinsic hand muscles and medial arm sensation.
An upper trunk lesion would weaken the biceps and brachioradialis and depress the biceps reflex, and would not weaken the finger extensors.
A middle trunk lesion produces radial-type extensor weakness but spares the deltoid and teres minor.
explanation.key_point: Posterior cord lesions combine axillary and radial deficits (deltoid, teres minor, triceps, wrist and finger extensors) with sparing of the biceps.

source_quote: thenar wasting and paresis (median innervation) may be prominent, whereas ulnar-supplied muscles are spared
vignette: A 31-year-old woman with a cervical rib has intermittent pain along the ulnar border of the hand and the medial forearm. Examination shows wasting and weakness of the thenar muscles. The hypothenar and interossei muscles have normal strength.
question: Which structure is most likely involved?
options: Median nerve at the wrist
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
C8-derived fibers of the lower trunk at the thoracic outlet
Ulnar nerve at the elbow
Posterior cord in the axilla

explanation.why_correct: In the rare neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome the lower trunk or medial cord is involved, with pain referred to the ulnar border of the hand and medial forearm. When only the C8 fibers are affected, thenar wasting (median innervation, predominantly C8) may be prominent while ulnar-supplied muscles (C8 and T1) are spared.
distractors: A lesion of the median nerve at the wrist would not explain pain and sensory symptoms along the medial forearm and ulnar border of the hand.
An upper trunk lesion causes deltoid, biceps and brachioradialis weakness, not thenar wasting.
An ulnar neuropathy would weaken the hypothenar and interossei muscles, which are normal here.
A posterior cord lesion causes axillary and radial deficits and does not cause thenar wasting.
explanation.key_point: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome involves the lower trunk or medial cord and may show thenar wasting with sparing of ulnar-supplied hand muscles.

source_quote: With metastatic disease, the lower trunk (C8-T1) is predominantly or exclusively involved, severe pain is present at onset, and Horner syndrome is common.
vignette: A 52-year-old woman treated for breast cancer with radiotherapy presents with severe pain at onset in the medial arm and hand. She then develops weakness of finger flexion and intrinsic hand muscles, with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome. There is no arm lymphedema.
question: Which cause of the plexopathy is more likely?
options: Radiation-induced injury of the upper trunk
Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome)
Diabetic cervical radiculoplexus neuropathy
Positioning trauma during anesthesia
Metastatic or recurrent tumor involving the lower trunk

explanation.why_correct: With metastatic disease the lower trunk (C8-T1) is predominantly or exclusively involved, severe pain is present at onset, and Horner syndrome is common. Radiation plexopathy more often involves the upper trunk or entire plexus, with paresthesias and weakness more prominent than pain and with progressive lymphedema.
distractors: Radiation plexopathy more often affects the upper trunk or entire plexus, causes less pain at onset, and is more often associated with arm lymphedema.
Neuralgic amyotrophy is idiopathic or follows viral illness or immunization, and mainly affects proximal shoulder and arm muscles, not a lower trunk pattern with Horner syndrome.
Diabetic cervical radiculoplexus neuropathy occurs in patients with diabetes, involves upper, middle and lower segments equally, and no diabetes is described.
Positioning trauma usually gives painless motor deficits at the C5-C7 levels.
explanation.key_point: Lower trunk involvement, severe early pain and Horner syndrome favor tumor over radiation as the cause of a brachial plexopathy.

source_quote: Neck metastases, usually from breast cancer, may involve the phrenic nerve along with the sympathetic chain and recurrent laryngeal nerve
vignette: A 56-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer has exertional dyspnea and hoarseness. Examination shows ipsilateral ptosis and miosis, a paralyzed vocal cord on laryngoscopy, and an elevated hemidiaphragm on the same side. There are no limb weakness or sensory deficits.
question: Which lesion best explains this combination of findings?
options: Metastatic infiltration of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus
Idiopathic neuralgic amyotrophy of the upper trunk
Thoracic outlet compression by a cervical rib
Compression of the lumbosacral trunk
Neck metastases involving the phrenic nerve, sympathetic chain and recurrent laryngeal nerve

explanation.why_correct: Neck metastases, usually from breast cancer, can involve the phrenic nerve together with the sympathetic chain and the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing diaphragmatic paralysis, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ipsilateral vocal cord paralysis (Payne syndrome).
distractors: Lower trunk infiltration would cause hand weakness and sensory loss, which are absent here, and would not paralyze the vocal cord or diaphragm.
Neuralgic amyotrophy causes painful shoulder and proximal arm weakness, and would not cause a vocal cord palsy with Horner syndrome.
Thoracic outlet compression gives arm pain and hand weakness or vascular signs, not vocal cord paralysis or diaphragm paralysis.
The lumbosacral trunk lies in the pelvis and has no relation to the diaphragm, vocal cord or eye.
explanation.key_point: Phrenic palsy plus ipsilateral Horner syndrome and vocal cord paralysis suggests neck metastases (Payne syndrome).

source_quote: A flail foot results because of paralysis of the dorsiflexors and plantar flexors of the foot.
vignette: A 63-year-old woman with a pelvic neoplasm has a foot that cannot be dorsiflexed or plantar flexed. She also has weak knee flexion, hip extension and hip abduction, an absent ankle jerk, sensory loss over the posterior thigh and sole, and difficulty controlling her bladder. Quadriceps strength, hip adduction and the patellar reflex are normal.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Lumbar plexus
Sacral plexus
Common peroneal nerve at the fibular head
L5 nerve root
Femoral nerve

explanation.why_correct: Sacral plexus lesions produce motor loss in the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal and sciatic distributions, with a flail foot, weak hamstrings, weak hip extension and abduction, sensory loss in the sciatic and posterior femoral cutaneous territories, a lost Achilles reflex, and sphincter difficulty from pudendal nerve involvement.
distractors: A lumbar plexus lesion affects the femoral and obturator distributions (hip flexion, knee extension, adduction) and the patellar reflex, which are normal here.
A common peroneal lesion would cause foot drop but not plantar flexion weakness, a lost ankle jerk, hip weakness or sphincter symptoms.
An L5 root lesion would not explain plantar flexion weakness, bladder dysfunction, or posterior thigh sensory loss.
A femoral neuropathy affects the quadriceps and patellar reflex, which are normal here.
explanation.key_point: Sacral plexus lesions cause a flail foot, gluteal and hamstring weakness, a lost Achilles reflex and possible pudendal sphincter signs.

source_quote: the descending fetal head may compress the lumbosacral trunk as it passes over the pelvic rim
vignette: A short-statured woman has a prolonged labor and vaginal delivery. The next day she has a unilateral foot drop with weak ankle dorsiflexion, eversion and inversion, and sensory loss in an L5 distribution. Knee extension and hip adduction are normal.
question: Which structure was most likely compressed?
options: Lumbosacral trunk at the pelvic rim
Femoral nerve under the inguinal ligament
Obturator nerve in the obturator canal
Entire lumbar plexus within the psoas muscle
Pudendal nerve (S1-S4)

explanation.why_correct: During labor the descending fetal head may compress the lumbosacral trunk as it passes over the pelvic rim. Intrapartum maternal lumbosacral plexopathy usually occurs in short women and presents with weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, eversion and inversion with L5 sensory loss, and an almost always unilateral foot drop.
distractors: The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps (knee extension), which is normal here.
The obturator nerve supplies the thigh adductors, which are normal here.
A lesion of the entire lumbar plexus would weaken hip flexion, knee extension and adduction, not just the foot.
A pudendal lesion produces perineal and sphincter symptoms, not foot drop.
explanation.key_point: Postpartum unilateral foot drop with L5 sensory loss in a short woman points to compression of the lumbosacral trunk by the fetal head.

source_quote: The diagnosis of retroperitoneal hematoma must be suspected in any patient receiving anticoagulants who complains of back, groin, thigh, or leg pain.
vignette: A 70-year-old man receiving intravenous heparin develops severe groin and thigh pain. His leg is held flexed and externally rotated, and extending it worsens the pain. There is suprainguinal tenderness, quadriceps weakness and a decreased patellar reflex, and his hematocrit is falling.
question: What is the most likely cause of his femoral nerve dysfunction?
options: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy
Tumor infiltration of the lumbosacral plexus
Radiation-induced lumbosacral plexopathy
Retroperitoneal hematoma
Compression of the lumbosacral trunk by the fetal head

explanation.why_correct: A retroperitoneal hematoma must be suspected in any anticoagulated patient with back, groin, thigh or leg pain. Findings include suprainguinal tenderness, pain on leg extension, flexion and external rotation of the limb, femoral, obturator and lateral femoral cutaneous neuropathies, and evidence of blood loss with falling hematocrit.
distractors: Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy is subacute and associated with weight loss and type 2 diabetes, not anticoagulation and falling hematocrit.
Tumor infiltration produces insidious pain over weeks to months, not an acute presentation with blood loss.
Radiation plexopathy causes indolent, usually distal leg weakness, not acute pain with a falling hematocrit.
Fetal head compression applies only during labor and affects the lumbosacral trunk, producing foot drop.
explanation.key_point: Acute groin or thigh pain, a flexed and externally rotated leg and a falling hematocrit in an anticoagulated patient suggest a retroperitoneal hematoma.
